maintopic: SEIZURE OF THE SCHOONER ' AGNES DONAHOE.'
speechtext:
I wish once more to bring to the attention of the government the case of the ' Agnes Donahoe,' a sealing vessel which was seized some time ago by the Uruguayan government. I received a letter in April last which contained some particulars that I think I have not yet communicated to the House. I need not read the whole letter but briefly the particulars are these :	The ' Agnes Donahoe ' was seized
for alleged poaching on November 10th, 1904, by the Uruguayan authorities and taken to Montevideo where she is still lieid with a crew of twenty men ; the schooner was several miles from land when she was seized ; she was then under sail with all bauds on board. Proceedings seem to have been taken by the Uruguayan government which made the charge that the ship was then fitted out and on her way to raid seal rookeries belonging to the government of Uruguay. They asked the captain to show his authority for sealing iu the southern seas. Before going on this voyage or any voyage, the owners of the ship had endeavoured to obtain information as to whether or not any sealing license was necessary, and on the 11th day of October, 1900, they received from John Hardie. Acting Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa the following telegram ;
Sealing licenses issue! only at Victoria ancf Vancouver under Paris award. No such licenses are necessary in Atlantic or in Pacific south of 35th degree north latitude.
The owners had a great many communications with the British Consul who thought there was no ground whatever for the

seizure by the Uruguayan authorities. The letter which I have is a little involved in the way in which it deals with the question, but another complaint which the owners make is this :	They started their business
in 1900 and they shipped the skins from Port Stanley, Falkland Islands, to London. At the personal request of the governor of the islands, in order as he said to protect the interests of Chili and Argentine, and in opposition to a petition signed by the people of the islands, a tax of 10 shillings per skin was imposed on all skins shipped from that port by Canadian sealers. This compelled them to give ms that port and to ship from another port, and during the year 1904 Brazil accorded to them the privilege denied to them at a British port. They preferred Port Stanley, the British port, as it is cooler and the skins did not deteriorate there as they do in the port to which access is given to them by Brazil. They were informed, in fact they have a cable from London from persons there wishing to purchase sealing schooners, in which these persons in London state that they have a concession to seal at Cape Horn, and these owners-perhaps without foundation, do not know about that-suggest that the impost of 10 shillings per skin was imposed in the interests of persons in London. Of course this is rather a grave suggestion, and I only mention it because it is emphatically stated by my correspondents, who are members of a respectable firm in Halifax.

maintopic: SEIZURE OF THE SCHOONER ' AGNES DONAHOE.'
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman repeat that ?

maintopic: SEIZURE OF THE SCHOONER ' AGNES DONAHOE.'
speechtext: He says there is an impost of ten shillings per skin if they should ship their skins from Port Stanley, and that it is imposed in the interest of persons in London who desire to go into the same trade. That is a very grave statement. and I only mention it because it comes from very respectable men, engaged m business in Halifax and personally known to myself and also no doubt known to the Minister of Finance. If necessary I will send their names to the First Minister. That is_ the position of these men. Ihey complain of an unlawful seizure, -they complain that their vessel was detained for months, and the information came from the Minister of Marine and h isheries himself that the vessel was detained during this very long period in order that the Uruguayan legislative body, whatever it is, might pass a law for the purpose of dealing with the case. The second complaint is that having gone into the southern seas, upon representation that no license was necessary, their vessel was seized while a long distance out at sea, on the pretense, which they declare absolutely unfounded, that she was engaged in an attempt to poach in rookeries belonging to the government of that country. The tel-'"'hick came to me last evening from Halifax is as follows :

maintopic: SEIZURE OF THE SCHOONER ' AGNES DONAHOE.'
speechtext:
Captain * Agnes Donahoe ' sentenced three years penal servitude mates one year, crew six months ship confiscated.
If the facts are as detailed by these men, it seems to me that no time should be lost in making the most urgent possible representations to the British government. A Canadian ship was seized on the high seas and held in custody about six months. The captain and crew were virtually detained as prisoners with the result that the ship is confiscated, the captain sentenced to three years penal servitude, the mates to one year, and the crew to six months. Under the circumstances there does not appear any justification for the course pursued by the government of Uruguay ; and it further, appears that whatever representations may have been made by this government to the British government in the matter do not seem to have produced a very profound impression on the imperial authorities. It may be, as my correspondent suggests that the British government thought no further action could be taken until the decision of the courts had been obtained. But now they have the decision of the courts pronounced in a fashion which should stimulate this government and the foreign office into some degree of activity. Nothing so bad as this took place in connection with the seizures in the Behring sea ; and I sincerely trust that whatever representations may have been made in the past, they will be renewed in a still more urgent form, and it may be ascertained whether or not there is some redress.

I have nothing to say, and my hon. friend has said nothing, as to the proceedings of the court; but it seems a very extreme and hard sentence on the Captain that he should be condemned to three years penal servitude. There is just one point which I want to clear with regard to the responsibility of this government. My hon. friend states that the owners of this schooner applied to this government in 1900 to know whether a license was required and they were told that none was necessary south of such a degree of latitude. I do not know what answer was given, but

there seems to have been misapprehension between the owner of the schooner and the officers of the department who gave that information, because the licenses which we issue at Victoria and Vancouver are licenses under the Paris award, passed in 1794, as the result of the Arbitration treaty.

speechtext:
A few days ago the hon. member for North i Toronto (Mr. Foster) asked a question with regard to a man named Nixon at Macleod. In reply to that question I beg to say that a sub-agency of Dominion lands was opened in Macleod on the 3rd May, 1899, with Joseph Nixon as sub-ao-ent. From the date of his appointment^ to the 1st April, 1900, he was paid by commission. From the 1st April, 1900, to the 1st June, 1902, his salary was at the rate of $25 a month. From the 1st June, 1902, up to the time of his resignation on the 31st March, 1905, his salary was at the rate of $50 per month. On the 1st Octo-

her, 1901, he was appointed caretaker of the immigration building at Macleod. and land guide for the district, at the rate of $10 per month. This sum was increased to $25 per month on the 1st May, 1904, which rate of pay continued until his resignation.
Owing to Mr. Nixon's connection with the immigration branch as caretaker of the hall and land guide, a good part of his time was employed in outside work, and he left his office in charge of his son. Some time in the month of March, 1905, information was received by the department that there were some irregularities in the conduct of the office at Macleod. The inspector of agencies was immediately wired to investigate and report. His report showed that there was a shortage of moneys which should have been returned to the agent of Dominion lands at Lethbridge to the amount of $499.05. Mr. Nixon's son, who had been in charge of the office, left for parts unknown on the 15th March. This was the first intimation Mr. Nixon had that anything was wrong with his accounts. He immediately paid over to the agent of Dominion lands at Lethbridge the sum of $499.05, the amount found to be short by the inspector's report. He also handed in his resignation as sub-agent of Dominion lands at Lethbridge, and upon the recommendation of the inspector that sub-agency was closed.
The immigration branch of the department required the services of a man as checker of immigrants on the train between Macleod and Fernie, and on the 20th April, 1905, the commisisoner at Winnipeg was instructed to engage Mr. Nixon temporarily for this week. Had Mr. Nixon not been engaged it would have been necessary for us to secure the services of some other man. Before the date at which it was decided to employ Mr. Nixon as checker on the train, the immigration building at Macleod had been closed, therefore, Mr. Nixon's services as caretaker were no longer required. The only salary he receives now from the department is $75 per month as checker on the train between Macleod and Fernie, together with his actual travelling expenses. Fp to the time the report was received in the department as to the above shortage, Mr. Nixon's services as sub-agent were satisfactory, and ns no reflection was cast upon his character by the said report, it was considered that there could be no objection to tlie department employing him again in a different capacity.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the

Day are called, I would like to make an explanation with respect to a question raised by my hon. friend from South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) in connection with the freight rates on the Intercolonial. On the 27th of April my hon. friend spoke of an alleged increase an these rates. I quote from the hon. gentleman's remarks as they appear at page 4997 of the Revised ' Hansard ' :
Some time ago, I made the statement to the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmer-son) that since the Railway Commission was formed we were paying a higher rate on our goods than formerly. He stated that there had been no advance on the Intercolonial Railway.
And he then goes on to read a letter which he received from a gentleman who does business in the city of St. John. I shall not take up the time of the House by repeating that letter. Later on my hon. friend states :
He explained that the rate to Fredericton had been 58 cents per hundred pounds-a pretty round, full rate, I should say. They hilled the goods to Dernoxville, and they went from Len-noxville to Fredericton. But since my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emerson), acquired the Canada Eastern Railway, the Grand Trunk hare instructions to ship everything to Fredericton over the Intercolonial Railway, and the rate to be paid is 66 cents per hundred pounds. If the minister desires to verify the figures, he will find them in Grand Trunk supplementary tariff D. G. M. 4, page 10.
My hon. friend also referred to another case and went ou to state as follows :
We had the misfortune to lose by fire our carriage works at Brockville. We had a contract *with the Nova Scotia Steel Co. for a quantity of tire steel. It happened that a car came immediately after the Are. We could not use it at Brockville, so we instructed the railway people to give instructions to have it forwarded to Gananoque, where the tiring had to be done after the Are. The rate from the works in Nova Scotia to Brockville "was 25 cents per hunderd pounds. The car arriving at Broek-ville was not unloaded, but was simply forwarded 30 miles to Gananoque, and when it arrived there, the rate charged was 37* cents per hundred pounds-or 12 cents per hundred pounds for the 30 mile haul from Brockville to Gananoque. We have refused to accept the car, and the question is in dispute. A few days ago we received a circular headed ' Canadian Freight Association '. It appears that nearly all the railways in Canada and the United States have joined this combine in freight rates. I see that the Intercolonial, under the direction of the Minister of Railways, is a member of this combine for Axing and settling rates.
He then goes ou to read an extract from a circular which was issued by certain railways. I took this matter up with the general traffic manager of the Intercolonial, and desire now to read his answer and to have it placed on record as an explanation, not merely of the charge made that there had been an increase of freight rates on the Intercolonial, but as an explanation
with respect to the tariff charge on the cars from Brockville to Gananoque. The letter I am reading is written by Mr. E. Tiffin, the general traffic manager of the Intercolonial, and is dated 11th May, 1905 :
Dear Mr. Emmerson,
Referring to the revised edition of the House of Commons Debates, Thursday, April 27th, which you sent me, and that part of it having particular reference to the statements made by Mr. George Taylor, M.P., for South Leeds.
I have to say that the statement made by Mr. Taylor as to there being any advance in the Intercolonial rates to Fredericton is not correct in so far as the Intereolonian Railway is concerned. You will remember that the case to which Mr. Taylor refers is one over which a good deal of correspondence took place with the Grand Trunk, Canadian PaeiAe, and Messrs. A. F. Randolph & Co., of Fredericton, and I think a complete answer to Mr. Taylor's statement is contained in my letter to you of January 10th last, in which I inclosed you a copy of a letter which I had written to Messrs. A. F. Randolph & Co. on this subjtcet. and I cannot do better than send you herewith copies of the correspondence referred to, which I think will give a complete answer to Mr. Taylor's statement.
In regard to that part of Mr. Taylor's complaint in which he refers to a shipment of a car of steel shipped by the Nova Scotia Steel & Coal Co., which was consigned to them at Brockville, and was afterwards forwarded to Gananoque, we have nothing whatever to do with it. The property was consigned to Brockville, it was way-billed to Brockville and carried to Brockville, and after its arrival at Brockville I judge from Mr. Taylor's statement that they required the car sent on to Gananoque. This being so, it became a question entirely with the Grand Trunk as to what charges they should make from Brockville to Gananoque, and it being a local shipment purely and entirely subject to Grand Trunk control, the question of the rate of freight to be charged from Brockville to Gananoque was one in which they alone had anything to say, and if Mr. Taylor has any complaint it is against the Grand Trunk Railway and not against the Intercolonial, because on the arrival of the car at Brockville all connection that the Intercolonial had with the shipment ceased.
Again, in Mr. Taylor's remarks he states, in reference to the freight from Nova Scotia to Brockville as against Pittsburg to Brockville that the rate of 20i cents from Pittsburg to Brockville is much less than the rate of 25 cents from Nova Scotia to Brockville, and goes on to say that the distance from Pittsburg to Brockville is less than it is from Trenton, N.S., to Brockville. This statement is not correct, because the mileage from Pittsburg to Brockville is 595 miles, while the mileage from Trenton, N.S.. to Brockville is 931 miles thereby showing that the rate from Trenton to Brockville is very much less, according to the mileage, than is ihe late from Pittsburg to Brockville, inasmuch as the 25 cents rate Trenton to Brockville is equal to 54.-IOO of a cent per ton per mile, while the rate of 20J cents from Pittsburg to Brockville is equal to 77-100 of a cent per ton per mile. You will see from this that the rate : from Pittsburg is much higher per ton per mile than is the rate from Trenton.

In regard to Mr. Taylor's statement as to the circular issued by the Railways addressed to the shippers, I cannot do better than inclose you herewith a copy of the circular, which fully explains the necessity for its issue, and when read altogether as a circular instead 'of taking extracts from it, surely it is not a circular that any shipper who desires to deal fairly with the Railways can object to. In fact, it is a protection to the shipper who conducts his business in an honest, straightforward manner, as against the shipper who does not, and the circular is one which, in my opinion, cannot reasonably be found fault with.
The rest of Mr. Taylor's remarks seem to concern only the acts of Railways other than the Intercolonial, and therefore, I assume, are not matters upon which you desire that I should express an opinion.
Yours truly,
General Traffic Manager.

Emmerson,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa, Ont.
I will rend the circular letter a little later, placing them all on ' Hansard.' But I will now read the letter referred to In Mr. Tiffin's letter just read, dated 10th January, 1905, written by Mr. Tiffin to myself :
Dear .Mr. Emmerson,

I beg to return you herewith the letter addressed to you by Messrs. A. F. Randolph & ,Sons, in which they attach copy of a letter they wrote me on January 4th relative to the recent advance made in the rates to Fredericton, and in reply to your request for an explanation, I cannot do better than inclose copy of my reply to Messrs. Randolph & Sons under date of January 6-th.
I am certainly at a loss to understand why Mr. Randolph should make any reference to the Intercolonial sanctioning the tariffs, because in view of the letters which have passed between myself and Mr. Raudolph he must have known that we vigorously opposed and did everything in our power to prevent the discrimination against Fredericton. I have written any number of letters to the Canadian Pacific, also to Mr. Loud of the Grand Trunk, in which we protested and protested most vigorously, against the unfair position in which they were placing Fredericton. At one time we thought we had the Grand Trunk won over to our views, but we were disappointed inasmuch as after Mr. Loud intimated to Mr. Wallace that he would not back up the action of the Canadian Pacific, he turned completely around and turned us down In our request for justice to Fredericton.
I cannot do better than inclose you herewith a copy of a telegram which I sent Mr. Loud on the 19th of October, also copy of my wire to him of the 28th October. These go to show that every effort was made that we could make to induce the Grand Trunk to meet our request and not permit of any advance over St. John rates to be made to Fredericton, that is, that wherever rates 'were current to St. John from points west of Montreal should also apply to Fredericton. We, however, failed to get the I Grand Trunk to como in with our views ; had they done so, there would have been no change in the rates, and it simply goes to show the Mr. EMMERSON.
understanding between the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific as to the rates that shall be current from west of Montreal. Where we control the situation ouselves, as we do out of Fredericton on west bound business, we put in the St, John rates flat, and where we control the rates east hound, as we do out of Montreal, Quebec, &c., we made the St. John rates apply east bound ; and the whole trouble is the points west of Montreal reached by the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk from which we were unable to get them to adopt our suggestion and apply the St. John rates.
As. stated in my letter to Randolph & Sons of the 6th of January (copy attached) I do not see what more we can do. If it is as I was advised, that in view of getting flour carried to Fredericton at the same rates as to St. John, they were willing to put up with the advance in the class rates on general merchandise, I think it is rather late in the day now l'or Randolph & Sons to come back at us and find fault with us for sanctioning a tariff which we did not sanction, but which, if I am correctly advised, at the meeting between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Fredericton merchants, the Fredericton merchants themselves agreed to.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) E. TIFFIN,
General Traffic Manager.
I now read from a letter dated 6th January, 1905, signed by E. Tiffin, general traffic manager, and addressed to A. F. Randolph & Sons, Fredericton, N.B., as follows :
Moncton, N.B., 6th January, 1905. Messrs. A.-'F. Randolph & Sons,
Fredericton, N.B.
Dear Sirs,-I have your favour under date of the 4th of January, relative to Fredericton rates, and. you will pardon me if I say that I am certainly very much surprised at its contents.
You have evidently overlooked the voluminous correspondence which we previously had on the subject of the Fredericton rates, more particularly my letter to you of November 3rd and your reply of November 7th.
I can only repeat that at the time the Fredericton rates were advanced over those of St. John, we made every effort possible with our connections, hoth'the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railways, to bring about a result that would have been satisfactory to the Fredericton people. We failed ; both of our connections refusing to agree to our request that Fredericton should on no account be placed higher than St. John. Fredericton being a point on the Canadian Pacific as well as on this line, the Canadian Pacific being the short line have the right to name the rates, and as the traffic originates off this line we have no voice in the matter, excepting that we entered a strong protest against the injusiee to Fredericton. Having done this, we could do no more.
Then, after the correspondence I had with you, I understood that +he Fredericton Board of Trade, or the Fredericton merchants, had a meeting with Messrs. Bulling, Sutherland and Maclnnes of the Canadian Pacific, and that the Canadian Pacific conceded to you that St. John rates on flour and grain would apply to -Fredericton ; and I was advised ihat this concession on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway was satisfactory to the Fredericton people. I

understand that at this meeting the question of rates on class freights was discussed and that there was only one of the staple commodities, namely, sugar, and it was found not to be affected because the sugar was shipped from Halifax. I further understand that at this meeting it was fully explained that from the Canadian Pacific standpoint any change in the proposed class rates would affect them seriously, and that the Fredericton merchants or the Fredericton Board of Trade were satisfied to allow the difference in that class of rates to continue.
Now then, if this report of the meeting which was held between your people and the Canadian Pacific is true, how can you now complain of your being charged higher rates from Toronto to Fredericton than from Toronto to St. John ? If you will permit me to say so, I think you made a mistake, if I am correctly informed, when you agreed to allow the discrimination to continue in so far as the class rates are concerned. As the best evidence in the world that we did not permit that discrimination to points -which we actually controlled, I would say that we insisted upon the Moncton rates (which are the.same as St. John) applying to all intermediate points on the old Canada Eastern. This,
I understand, was objected to by the Canadian Pacific Railway, but notwithstanding their objection we carried our point. We could not, however, carry it to Fredericton because, as stated above, the Canadian Pacific Railway are the short line and therefore have the control of the rates. The Intercolonial Railway, therefore, should not be blamed for the existence of a condition which they could not control, but to prevent which they did all in their power to meet what I consider a fair and reasonable proposition, that is, that the St. John class and grain rates should apply to Fredericton.
I have looked up Mr. Wallace's letter of the 7th of November to which you refer, and while I admit that it is perhaps ambiguous, yet I do not take from it the inference that you do, that is, that had we asked our connections to make St. John rates apply to Fredericton, it would have been granted, because you must know from the previous correspondence we had that we made an urgent and imperative demand that the St. John rates should apply to Fredericton. ,
In view of the fact of it having been stated that your people agreed with the Canadian Pacific representatives that if you obtained the same rates on flour and grain as were current to St. John for local delivery, you would noty press the question of the class rates, I do not see how I can again approach the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific with a view of having this discrimination removed, and in fact if you have agreed with the Canadian Pacific as it is stated that you have, that the class rates to Fredericton may be higher than to St. John, it seems to me that you have taken the ground from under your feet if it is the intention to apply to the Railway Commission for relief.
I would like very much to have gone to Fredericton to discuss this matter with you and with your board of trade, but as I am obliged to leave for Montreal early next week, I regret that I will not have the opportunity of doing so.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) E. TIFFIN,
General Traffic Manager.
Now, to show that a protest was made by the Intercolonial Railway, I will read the following telegram of the 19th October,
1901, signed by E. Tiffin, our traffic manager, and addressed to Mr. J. W. Loud, who is the general traffic manager of the Grand Trunk Railway at Montreal. It reads as follows :
Moncton, 19th October, 1904.
J. W. Loud, Montreal, P.Q.
I have already advised you that there was no agreement as between myself and the Canadian Pacific Railway on Fredericton rates. As the traffic originates on your line and the Canadian Pacific west of Montreal, the usual custom is that it rests with yourself and the Canadian Pacific Railway as ro what the rates shall be. We protest against any advance to Fredericton over St. John rates. This is all we can do. What I would like to know now is inasmuch as you have not put in advanced flour rates, if you propose to advance them, upon what date does the advance come into effect.
(Sgd.) E. TIFFIN.
The2 other telegram between the same parties and which bears date the 28th October, 1904, reads as follows :
Moncton, 28th October, 1904.
J. W. Loud, Montreal, P.Q.,
Your telegram date re Fredericton rates. I still consider as a matter of justice and right that Fredericton rates should be on the basis of St. John and not any higher, in view of local changes made by Canadian Pacific from St. John and Fredericton; and in view also of the reduction in their flour rates to their points North of Macadam Junction, this advance to Fredericton can have no other effect than that of crippling Fredericton as a distributing centre. We still protest against the action of the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific in regard to Fredericton rates.
-	E. TIFFIN.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I presume the hon. minister intends to conclude with a motion?
I am making this statement in answer to a statement made by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor). This is simply information.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I shall move the adjournment of the House if he does not.

With the permission of the House I simply wish to give this information. I think it is fair to the members. fair to my hon. friend and it certainly is something that is due to the business'interests of the country.

That is all right, but the minister must recollect that there will be a right of reply. He is taking up arguments made in a previous debate by the
(ill 9

lion, member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) ; be is controverting these arguments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Me has only read letters so far.
I am merely reading letters, not arguing.
It does not make any difference whether the hon. gentleman makes the argument himself or does it by reading letters to this House.

These are simply statements of fact giving information with respect to the freight tariff of the Intercolonial Railway in answer to an inquiry made by an hon. member of this House. This circular letter reads as follows :
To shippers, consignees, agents, or whom it may concern:
The railway companies regret to say that they find the practice of false classification, false representation of the contents of packages, false report of weight, &c., continues unabated. It is therefore thought desirable that the attention of shippers should be called to the provisions of the law on the subject. Section 279, subsections two and three, of the Railway Act, 1903, are as follows:-
2.	Any company or any officer or agent thereof or any person acting for or employed by the company, who, by means of false billing, false classification, false report of weight or by any other device or means, shall knowingly, wilfully, or shall willingly suffer or permit any person or persons to obtain transportation for goods at less than the required tolls then authorized and in force on the railway of the company, shall for each offence be liable to a penalty of not exceeding one thousand dollars nor less than one hundred dollars.
3.	Any person or any officer or agent of any incorporated company who shall deliver goods for transportation to the company, or for whom as consignor or consignee the company shall transport goods, who shall knowingly or wilfully, by false billing, false classification, false weighing, false representation of the contents of the package or false report of weight, or by any other device or means, whether with or without the consent or connivance of the company, its agent or agents, obtain transportation for such goods at less than the regular tolls then authorized, and in force on the railway shall for each offence be liable to a penalty 6f not exceeding one thousand dollars nor less than one hundred dollars. The board may make regulations providing that any such person or company shall, in addition to the regular toll, be liable to pay to the company a further toll not exceeding fifty per cent of the regular charge. The company may, and when ordered by the board shall, open and examine any package, box. case or shipment for the purpose of ascertaining whether this subsection has been violated.
The practice of false classification, &e., not only deprives the railway companies or revenue to^ which they are justly entitled, but places shippers who do not adopt such devices, and who are averse to defying the law, at a most unfair disadvantage. The railway companies hope it is only necessary to bring this Mr. FOSTER.
matter to the attention of shippers to have the abuse entirely discontinued.
H. R. PATRIARCHE, Sec.-Treas. Western Lines, Winnipeg.
JOHN EARLS, Sec.-Treas. Eastern Lines, Toronto.
Issued April 3rd, 1905.

Is there a joint tariff arrangement between the Intercolonial Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, and is that tariff arrangement under the control of the commissioners ?

As I am advised there is no such tariff arrangement. The Intercolonial Railway makes its own rates with respect to its own portion of the line, but it is bound to accept the joint arrangement which exists between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway on freight originating west of Montreal, * the western terminus of the Intercolonial.

If I remember the Act that joint tariff must be approved of by tiie commissioners. I knew that the Intercolonial Railway tariff was not subject to the commissioners, but the joint tariff or the tariff which either of the roads could charge was subject to the approval of the commission. I cannot understand how it is that these railway companies vary outside of the tariff which is approved of by the commission.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood that the hon. minister intended to conclude with a motion.

I thought I was simply giving information to the House which was asked, and that under the rules of the House such departmental information could always be given at tliis stage of the proceedings of the House. I may be incorrect in that belief. I think perhaps, instead of making a motion I should apologize for taking up the time of the House.'
You ought to do both.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that in order to have the proceedings of the House properly in order the hon. minister should conclude with a motion.
I bow to the Speaker's ruling and I will conclude with that motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Ennnerson moves that the House do now adjourn.
Carried.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would like to inquire from the premier through you, why it is that the members of the opposition should not be entitled to the same courtesies that ministers expect for themselves. If a

member of the opposition brings up some trivial incident a minister will squeal like a little pig and say : I did not know it was coming up. The Minister of Railways brings up a matter here affecting as he says the bon. member for Leeds and this is the first; intimation I had that he was going to bring it forward. I am not going to complain, I think I shall give him a Roland for his Oliver before I sit down. The disc'ussion he referred to took place on April 27, and was a general discussion for the benefit of railways in general. During that discussion I referred to a case in point and expressed the hope that the Railway Commission which the government have established would look into the matter. The case in point was the shipment of our goods from Gananoque to Fredericton. Until the hon. gentleman acquired the Canada Eastern Railway our rate via Lennoxville junction by the Canadian Pacific Railway, to Fredericton, was 55 cents per 100 pounds. Yet, when the Canada Eastern is acquired, the goods go to Lennoxville just the same and then over the Intercolonial Railway and we are charged 66 cents per 100 pounds. The Minister of Railways could not contradict the statement I made in reference to that. He told me he would get the information and let me know, and I thought we would have a talk about it, but instead of that for half an hour he reads these long documents and circulars which are not pertinent to the question, and he does it for the purpose of obstructing the business of the House. I challenge him or any one else in the employ of the railroad to contradict my statement. For years I shipped goods to Fredericton for 55 cents per 100 pounds, and now when they go over the Canada Eastern we are charged 66 cents.
He explained that they all went into a combine.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways referred to a carload of steel and he corroborated my statement in every particular, because the rate to Brockville was 25 cents, but when it came 30 miles further we were charged 12 cents extra or 37 cents in all. I want the matter to go before the Railway Commission so that we may know why, if the Intercolonial Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway can haul from Nova Scotia to Brockville for 25 cents per 100 pounds, we should be charged 12 cents extra for hauling it on the same car without unloading, only 30 miles further. I did state that we received a car from Pittsburg, Pa., at 20i cents per 100 pounds, and that I thought that was a lower rate than 37 cents from Nova Scotia to Gananoque. So it is. I was mistaken in thinking that the distance from Pennsylvania was further than from Nova Scotia^ but at all events the 37 cent rate from Nova Scotia is higher in proportion. We have another case in dispute with the 195
Grand Trunk. We got a carload of lumber the other day hauled 10 miles on the Grand Trunk Railway and 3 miles on a branch line, and they charged us $19 for hauling that car of lumber. In view of such outrageous charges the Railway Commission should at once deal with the matters which were brought to the attention of the House on the 28th of April by the report of the Agricultural Committee. The statements I made on that day were intended for the Railway Commission that they might take action with regard to the hardships that shippers are subjected to. The Minister of Railways has not given a particle of eyi-ence to the House, that the Intercolonial is not charging 66 cents per 100 pounds for delivering goods from Gananoque at Fredericton, whereas before the Canada Eastern was acquired the rate was only 55 cents. He has not been able to deny my statement that this car of steel coming from Nova Scotia-intended for Brockville but ordered on-was hilled 25 cents to Brockville and for the 30 miles west an extra 12 cents or 37 cents in all. The minister got on ' Hansard ' a circular issued by the railway companies, not for the purpose of protecting shippers but for the purpose of protecting themselves, whereas the railways have their own protection in their own hands. In my opinion that circular is an insult to the shippers of this country. If you ship a parcel of goods and bill them to the railway companies at a certain weight, the railway companies have the scales and can test that weight, and my experience is that they generally charge more weight than there actually is. In the case of a carload of steel which came to us a short time ago, they tried to charge us for 1,940 pounds more freight than we actually paid for the number of pounds of steel which was weighed at both ends. We had that weight tested
That's a steal.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is a steal on the part of the railway people who charge more than the actual weight. The Minister of Railways presented this statement as a government statement to-day without moving the adjournment of the House, and he said he Avas simply making a statement of fact, but while the letters he read may be a statement of fact they are not facts, and he has not been able to contradict nay assertion. I want these matters dealt with by the Railway Commission, and it is for that reason I spoke the other day so that the Railway Commission may get down to business some time and see that there is a proper classification of freight and a proper charge made under it. X do not think the Railway Commission will allow the railways to charge 12 cents for a short haul of 30 miles and 25 cents for a long haul of 1,000 miles.

I wish to ask the Minister of Railways if the statement is true,



that the freight rates from points west of Montreal to Fredericton, via Intercolonial, are higher now than they were before the government acquired the Canada Eastern ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Certainly they are.
To Fredericton, so far as the Intercolonial is concerned, they are not higher.

My question was : are the rates now higher from points west of Montreal to Fredericton via the Intercolonial and Canada Eastern than these same were before the government acquired the Canada Eastern ?

They are from points west, because the arrangement was made before the Canada Eastern was acquired. That is not true with respect to the period since the Canada Eastern was acquired, because this change took place just previous to the acquisition of the Canada Eastern. My statement would be misleading if I said that this occurred since the Canada Eastern was acquired.
This discrimination which is complained of as against Fredericton has taken place since the government acquired the Canada Eastern.

No. Just previous to that the arrangement was made by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway. We took charge of the Canada Eastern in October, I think, and the arrangement I referred to was entered into in July or August of that year.

It was announced that the Intercolonial Railway was to take the railroad over on the 1st of September and all arrangements were made for taking over the road at that date ; in fact the cars were all ready and the Intercolonial Railway officials were there to take the road over. It was during that time as I understand that the announcement was made that the freight rates were to be increased, and it seems strange to me that the Canada Eastern should be able to procure a lower freight rate from points west of Montreal to Fredericton-the same rate as applies to St. John -and that the Intercolonial Railway, since it has obtained control of the Frederiction connection, has not been able to get as low a rate.

The rate was fixed by the western railways, when the Canada Eastern was owned by the Alexander Gibson Railway and Manufacturing Company. The rate that now exists to Fredericton over the Canada Eastern portion of the Intercolonial Railway was fixed at that time, previous to the acquisition and operation of the Canada Eastern by the Intercolonial Railway and the fact of the Intercolonial operating the road is in no way connected with the fact that the freight
rates were increased ; it is due to an arrangement entered into between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I would like to understand definitely from the Minister of Railways if that rate was agreed upon by the Canada Eastern Railway Company before the government acquired the road ?
I cannot say that, I do not know. I do not think it was, I do *not think they were called upon to do it at all.

It seems to me the government had it all in their hands with the commission. The commission had control over the tariff rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, and if they had made an arrangement that was too high all that was necessary was to appeal to the commission and have them revise the tariff. Now if that lay with the government and they found the rates too high when they took over the Canada Eastern it was in their own hands and they could have reduced the rates. So I think they are practically responsible for it no matter who is at fault whether it was the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific or the government railway.

I do not know that anybody is very seriously at fault in connection with the matter. The rate has been continued through to Fredericton because of an agreement entered into between the .Fredericton Board of Trade or the merchants of Fredericton and the Canadian Pacific Railway. They got certain concessions along another line whereby they were led to agree to these rates. That is the situation as I understand it. The tariffs have been filed and the Board of Trade of Fredericton could apply or application could be made by the Intercolonial Railway before the next tariffs are filed.
What about the shipping public ?

The shipping public can file a complaint also, but the Fredericton merchants and the Fredericton Board of Trade who are agreeable to this and who have apparently consented to it are not complaining and therefore action, I presume has not been taken.
Did I understand the Minister of Railways to say that the Gibson firm went into this arrangement previous to the time the government took over the Canada Eastern ?

I did not state that,
I said as a matter of fact I did not know whether they were a party to the arrangement or not, that it was an arrangement between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I was not

iaware that the 'Canada Eastern nr the Alexander Gibson Company were party to the arrangement.

The fact of the matter, as I understand the debate, is that the rates now are higher than they were some time ago, and higher than they were previous to the time the Canada Eastern was taken over by the government. If that is the case the Intercolonial Railway must have been parties to it because no freight could go over the Canada Eastern to Fredericton from points west of Montreal unless it went over the Intercolonial Railway.
Mr. EMM'ERSON. Whatever change was made in the rates to Fredericton was made previous to the acquisition of this road by the Intercolonial Railway, and therefore the Intercolonial Railway could not be a party to it because it did not own, operate or control the Canada Eastern at the time this arrangement was entered into.

The Minister of Railways does not understand me. This discussion is with regard to freight originating west of Montreal. That freight has to go over the Intercolonial Railway in order to reach Fredericton by the Canada Eastern ; it has to go over the Intercolonial Railway from Montreal to the junction point between that road and the Canada Eastern and therefore the Intercolonial Railway must have been a party to this advanced rate.
Mr. EMMBRlS'ON. No it was not ; the Intercolonial Railway as I have stated, protested against their entering into the agreement. I have shown the telegrams from the traffic manager of the Intercolonial Railway, I have shown his statement wherein he protested and showed that he was not a party to it.
To my mind he did not go far enough in these protests or he would have prevented the firm of Gibson & Sons from making such* an arrangement.
The Intercolonial Railway gets no more for its portion and has not increased its rate.

That may be but the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) is perfectly correct in this that you cannot have a through rate over four roads by reason of the concurrence of only three of these roads in the rate. There were four roads, the Canada Eastern, the Intercolonial Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, and the Canadian Pacific Railway. You cannot get a through rate over four or three of these roads without the concurrence of all the roads interested. There is another observation to be made in that connection, that it seems a remarkable thing that the Canada Eastern, after it had actually agreed to convey its road to the government, after the terms had been arranged 1951
with the exception of some trifling details, should undertake to enter into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway just on the eve of the sale of that road t<>
the government. it is to me absolutely inconceivable that the Canada Eastern Railway Company would have undertaken to assent to that alteration without the concurrence of the officers of the Intercolonial Railway, because I cannot think that the Company when it was about to part with the beneficial interests in that road undertook to enter into an agreement binding for a considerable time as to these through rates. 1 would think that notwithstanding the somewhat lengthly explanation which the minister has made to-day, he should give a fur ther explanation on that point and if necessary again move to adjourn the House.
Mr. EMM'ERSON. I have stated that I do not think that the Canada Eastern was a party to this arrangement. The arrangement was entered into between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, it inures to the advantage 'of the Canadian Pacific Railway, because clearly the traffic will not go by the Intercolonial Railway to Fredericton when it could go at a cheaper rate from Montreal direct to Fredericton by the Canadian Pacific Railway and certainly the Canadian Pacific Railway would not be a party to an arrangement that would work against its own interests. Therefore there is no such arrangement to-day. The Alexander Gibson Company was not a party to it, the Intercolonial Railway was not a party to it, but the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway in the carrying out of their western proposition, for what purpose I know not, have entered into an arrangement whereby the Intercolonial cannot get this western traffic from points west of Montreal and carry it at a rate as low as the Canadian Pacific have agreed to carry it.

If it is a through rate embracing the carriage of goods over a number of different railways, does it not come within the definition of what is called a joint traffic arrangement between these railways ? The hon. gentleman may say, so far as the Intercolonial is concerned, it is not subject to the provisions of the Railway Act, but if he takes the position he has taken just now, that it is solely due _ to the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, certainly they are subject to the Railway Commission.
Now you are on correct ground.

I have been on correct ground all along. If any one is on unsound ground it is the hon. minister from the time he began until he moved the adjournment of the House. Has the increase

of rates been approved by tbe Railway Commission in respect of tbe Canada Eastern Railway Company ? Was all this done on the very eve of the transfer of that railway to the government, and was the government asleep while all this was being done, although it knew that railway was going into its possession and would be operated by it in a very few days or1 weeks at the outside ? These are matters worthy of consideration, and if the minister this afternoon had given his attention to some of these matters rather than indulge in a very elaborate criticism of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), the House would be in a much better "position to come to a conclusion. I do not think the report was in very good taste. It is not usual to have the language of any member m this House, used in debate, made the subject of a somewhat controversial report issued by a departmental officer. But putting that consideration aside for the moment, the Minister of Railways ought to investigate this question a little further and find out whether this increase was made under the provisions of the law, and ascertain also whether or not it was made with the concurrence of the Canada Eastern Railway. He is not able to state to-day whether that is the case or not. And in particular, he should inform the House why it is that the rate which prevailed for a great number of years, while the Canada Eastern was operating that line, cannot prevail to-day when the government is operating lx. That, after all, Is the whole matter in question. The rate was a moderate and apparently a paying one, and was not increased while the Canada Eastern was operating the line, but upon the eve of the acquisition by the government of that line it is increased, and increased under circumstances the precise nature of which has not yet been imparted to this House.
This is the way in which the public have benefited.

This debate, it seems to me, is a great ado about nothing. In tbe first place, there is no grievance suffered by the merchants of Fredericton. That is shown by the fact that they have agreed to this extra rate in return for some consideration that they have obtained. We have had no complaints from the board of . trade or the merchants of Fredericton against the extra rate. As a matter of fact, I know that the rates oil flour are lower to-day in the maritime provinces than they have been, and the rate to Fredericton is lower than it was some time ago and the same to-day as it is to St. John.

I think that tile hon. member has overlooked entirely the correspondence read by the Minister of Railways. The letters he read contain very vigorous protests from the merchants of Federicton against the increased rate.

Everybody knows that tbe rate to Halifax is lower than it is to Fredericton, because at St. John you go right into water communication and have to compete with the water rate. The Canadian Pacific Railway can send its freight entirely over its own iline to Fredericton, and need not send it over the Intercolonial Railway at all. For myself, it is an extraordinary rate-it is too high. A.s a shipper, I know that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific

speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that a great portion of the goods shipped to Fredericton from Ontario are sold delivered, the shipper paying the freight ? Therefore, it is the shipper and not the merchant who has to complain.

We sell goods delivered, and if the freight is higher we charge more. If we could have them carried for nothing, we would sell our goods that much cheaper. There is a lot of work cut out for the Railway Commission. I believe that the local rates from one point to another in Ontario especially, are altogether too high. And I am sure that the Railway Commission, now that they have got into working order-I believe in giving them time-will investigate this matter and bring the railway to a more reasonable view.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) seems to think that the government have nothing to do with this that we have given virtual control of the railroad and the fixing of tariffs over to the Railway Commission ; and that, that having been done, the government may let things drift as they like. iMr. HAGGART. The observations of the Minister (Mr. Emmerson) are not pertinent to the argument I am making. LOGGIE (Northumberland, N.
B.). I would like to add a word to this discussion as I am more or less interested in the subject. I realize the circumstances that led up to this difficulty with the Canadian Pacific Railway. In fact I understand from their own agents that they were not satisfied with the former rates charged to Fredericton. They claim that Fredericton was not a competitive point, as St. John was, and they proposed raising the rates on flour and provisions, also the rates on commodities such as dry goods and general merchandise. This protest having been entered, a compromise was made, as I understand it, by which the previous rates should stand good on flour and commodities of that class, whereas on dry goods, textile products and so on, the rates were to be increased, above those they were giving to a competitive point, namely, St. John, New Brunswick. For that reason the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk entered into a traffic arrangement concerning local traffic, bv which they charged on commodities other than cereals, an increased rate. That agreement, or traffic arrangement, I have no doubt was confirmed by the Railway Commission at Ottawa, who, I suppose, con sidered it a reasonable one. But we must not forget that in freight arrangements it is very difficult to make rates that do not work hardly in some sections of the country. For example, let me point out to this House that to-day although Chatham is within nine miles of Chatham Junction, and Fredericton is within about 100 miles, yet freight is carried over the Grand Trunk and over the Intercolonial to Fredericton at a less rate than it is to Chatham. Now I wish particularly to state that that remark applies only to flour and that class of goods. Although is is hauled only nine miles from Chatham Junction into Chatham, we have to pav a higher rate than when it is hauled into Fredericton. Now the railway authorities answer us in this way, they say that B ieder-icton is nearer the point of production, and is a competitive point, and therefore we have not a right to the same rate that Fredericton has, because of our situation and our not being adjacent to the city of St. John. I can understand why the Fredericton merchants should claim the same rate of freight on heavy goods. But the difficulty in case seems to be that two great railway corporations have made a joint taritr on local freight which tariff has been confirmed by the Railway Commission. Now the question at issue is this : Is it a justifiable action on the part of the Railway Commission to confirm such a tariff which charges those extra rates ? If dry goods,
for example, can be hauled from the city of Toronto for 55 cents a hundred, and pay three roads out of that rate, why should two roads Charge 66 cents, 11 cents extra . Now we have to consider whether it would not be in the interest of the producer in the west and of the consumer in the east that the commission should revise that tariff and place Fredericton, so far as local trade F concerned, on the same basis that she was before. As I say, we have to pay on heavy goods coming into Chatham more freight than we pay on the same goods to Fredericton. although the haul is only nine miles from Chatham Junction to Chatham whereas it is over a hundred miles to Fredericton.
I understood the minister to say that the freight rate had been changed to Marysville, a point near Fredericton. Might 1 ask which point pays the higher freight, Fredericton or Marysville .

I think the papers which I read show that these points get uniform rates, all points from Chatham Junction through to Fredericton are given a uniform rate. If I mistake not, that rate is fixed on the basis of Moncton, and the rate to Moncton would be less than the rate to Fredericton because Moncton and St. John are placed on a par, that is to say, the rate which applies to St. John applies to Moncton. The contention of the Intercolonial was that the same rate should apply to Fredericton, while the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway act to the contrary. But where the Intercolonial have the control, that is up the river St. John to Gibson and Marysville, they continue the rate that had existed previously, that is, the same rate as the Moncton and St. John rate.

House in committee on Bill (No. 132) to amend the Government Railways Act.-Mr. Emmerson.
On section 1,

There are some slight amendments to be proposed to this section, most of which are merely intended to improve the wording and in order to make the meaning clear. The section as amended will read as follows :
The minister shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have for the purposes of and in connection with the business and traffic of any government railway in his charge or direction by virtue of the Government Railways Act, running powers over the whole or any portion of the lines of Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada between Montreal and Coteau Junction and over all or any of the lines and tracks of the system known as the Canada Atlantic Railway system extending from Coteau Junction to Depot Harbour and _the Georgian bay, as the said lines and tracks, including the said line between Montreal and Coteau Junction, now exist or as they are hereafter constructed, reconstructed, or extended.

In the discussion that took place on the first reading, this Bill seemed to be regarded as merely an option to the government to exercise or not to exercise running powers over this railway. It may be that in one sense the government may not be bound to exercise those running powers, but this section expressly and explicitly says that the government shall have running powers. Now if you enact a statute of that character will you not, by the very circumstance that the government is placed in the position to enter at any time and to exercise running powers, place the government and the country in the position of having to pay compensation to the Grand Trunk whether those running powers are exercised or not ? For example the property of the Grand Trunk Company subject to a

power of that kind which may be exercised under statute by the government would be a less valuable asset possibly to the company than it would be if it were subject to no such rights. It seems to me that the government by this legislation is doing something more than was suggested by the Prime Minister upon the introduction of this Bill and also by the Minister of Railways himself, and I would like to have a little more definite statement as to exactly what the result of this statute will be in this regard. Suppose this statute is passed and nothing more is done ; is it suggested that the Grand Trunk Railway whose property is made subject to this right will have no power of enforcing compensation against the government ? I would think that the opposite result is one which might be regarded as a fair result from the wording of this statute.

Or course my hon. friend is asking a legal question as to the legal consequences. My own view of the matter would be that the Grand Trunk Company couid not by any possibility have any legal, moral or equitable claim against the government of Canada. This is the parliament of Canada, it is the supreme power, it is the highest court in Canada, and it has power to deal with these matters and it enacts with respect to certain property that the government can, if it chooses, shall if it will exercise, and have the right to running powers and of course that section is to be interpreted in connection with the other clauses of the Act and no possible damages can accrue to the Grand Trunk Railway or to the other company, reading the whole Act together.

Have there been any negotiations, or correspondence, verbal or otherwise with the Grand Trunk or the Canada Atlantic as to the passage of this Act either before the acquisition by the Grand Trunk or the Canada Atlantic or since, and what is the effect of those negotiations and what is the purpose you intend to carry out under the Bill ?

Representatives of the company have been here when this Bill was before the committee and I think they addressed themselves to members of the Railway Committee when their Bill was before that body and this other proposition was spoken of. I think they are not disposed to favourably view this matter ; certainly they objected to the delay that resulted by reason of the desire which I expressed to have time to determine as to the character of the legislation that should be brought in giving running rights to the Intercolonial Railway.

I have not seen the remarks to which my hon. friend refers. I am speaking for my own department; there have been no negotiations, there is no bargain. I thought it was in the interest of the Intercolonial Railway that this Bill should be introduced, I obtained the consent of my colleagues, the Bill was prepared and is now before the committee, but not as the result of any bargain or any negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

I will make it wider, and say that so far as I know no negotiations of any kind were conducted with the government. The reason that I suggested the construction which I thought might be placed on the words of this Act is this : You have under section 1 a right created in this government-in respect of a railway owned by a private company. There is no ambiguity about the terms of that section. I shall omit the immaterial work : The minister shall have for the government railway running powers over that portion of the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Co-teau Junction and over all the lines and tracks of the system known as the Canada Atlantic Railway system. Then section 5 provides that the terms and conditions and the payment or compensation subject to which the said running powers may be so exercised shall be determined by the Board of Railway Commissioners. If you put those two provisions together, it seems to me that the Grand Trunk Railway will have the right to recover compensation against the Crown for that easement created in favour of the government over the property of the Grand Trunk Railway. For that reason I thought the Minister of Railways should be able to give us the opinion of the law officers of the Crown as to the effect of these two sections. The First Minister, on the first reading of the Bill, suggested that this was merely the creation of a right which might not be exercised for a long time, and which involved no obligation on the part of this country to pay anything. I am now stating it as my opinion that the converse is at least fairly arguable. I would like to know whether or not the minister has taken the opinion of the law officers of the Crown upon the construction of these two sections. If you create an easement and say that it shall be paid for according to the arbitrament of a certain tribunal, do you not permit the party against whom the easement is created to make application on its own initiative to the tribunal for the purpose of determining that compensation and incidentally the terms and conditions upon which this right shall be exercised. That seems an important question to be considered because you will find in the end that it is not the intention which the government may put into the Act, but that which is to be read in the words of the statute which will have effect and be carried out.

As was stated by the right hon. the First Minister at the first

reading, the exercise of these rights is not imperative. These rights need only be exercised when the government sees fit, and then the compensation will be determined by the Railway Commission. The question stated by my hon. friend was submitted by me to the Department of .Justice. That department drafted the Bill in accord with the expressed policy of the government. I would not presume to give a legal opinion upon these sections, but, as an individual. I would read them very differently from the way my hon. friend reads them. I would take into consideration the whole Bill and not pick out a word here and there in the different sections. According to the fifth section the running powers shall be subject to the terms and conditions to be fixed by the Railway Commission : but it is evident that the exercise of these powers is purely discretionary, and I cannot see how the Grand Trunk Railway could have any claim legal, equitable or moral against the government for the non-exercise of these powers and privileges, the exercise of which is discretionary with the government.

I stated that I was omitting the immaterial words, and I did not observe in any of the other sections anything which at all cuts down what is contained in the words I did read. This seems to me to be a statutory expropriation of an easement in respect of the Grand Trunk Railway lines between Montreal and Depot Harbour. The Bill contains also provisions for compensation. Would the Minister of Justice give us his opinion, if he has had the opportunity of examining the different sections of the Bill ?

On section 4,

I always understood that the Intercolonial Railway did not come under the control of the Railway Commission. On the first reading of this Bill I explained this clause. It would not be fair to the other railways running west of Montreal that they should be obliged to have their tariffs determined by the Railway Commission, while the Intercolonial Railway could use these very same tracks and adjust their tariffs at their own sweet will. While I objected to the freight tariffs of the Intercolonial Railway proper east of Montreal being subject to the Railway Commission, I felt that in the common interest it was only just that the rates west of Montreal should be approved by
the Railway Commission as in the case of other railways.

Yes, and we do not submit our through freight rates to the commission.

,It would be under the commission only so far as that portion of it west of Montreal is concerned.

Do I understand the minister to mean that the railway companies may make a joint tariff arrangement between themselves, and against the Intercolonial Railway as one of the railways affected, which does not need to submit its rates to the Railway Commission ?

The companies can admit a joint tariff but it is subject to the approval of the Railway Commission. The leader of the opposition stated on a former occasion that the Intercolonial Railway, in proposing to do a through business should be subject to the same authority as the other railways are with respect to the through business west of Montreal.
I do not think I said exactly that.
That is my impression.	.

If I remember correctly, I said that it seemed very anamalous that the Intercolonial Railway carrying through freight from the Georgian bay to the maritime ports should be subject to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission in respect to a portion of the distance and not in respect: to another portion of the distance. I did not see exactly how it could be worked out, because it seemed to me that the Railway Commission in determining a through rate must have regard to that portion ' of the line which is excluded from the provisions of the Railway Act. I confess that I do not yet see exactly how it can be worked out.

We propose to do a through freight business and a through and

local passenger business. It is proposed that the tariffs west of Montreal shall be subject to the Railway Board in order that there may be uniformity, and in order that the government railways should not be in a different position from the other railways. Then the commission would have jurisdiction from Georgian bay to Montreal on the freight that is carried on the Intercolonial Railway. That would be determined by the local rate, but the other railways would have the right to make a through rate and the Intercolonial Railway will not under this arrangement.
That through rate is subject to the supervision of the Railway Commission.

Not at all.
Surely my hon. friend will not dispute that ?

The Railway Commission has no jurisdiction at all over the rates on the Intercolonial Railway. Where do you give them jurisdiction over the through rates from the Georgian bay to' St. John or Halifax ?

Let me explain. We are not allowed to do any local freight traffic on the leased line. Section 3 says :
In exercising any such running powers the minister shall have the power to do a through freight and passenger business and a local passenger business.
We have not power to do a local freight business. Section 4 says :
The minister shall submit tariffs of the tolls to be charged for the carriage of traffic upon the said line and track to which said running powers extend, to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
The tariff so submitted must of necessity be a through tariff because the Intercolonial Railway can do no local freight business on the leased lines. The Intercolonial Railway would be compelled to file its tariff on that section with the Railway Commission just the same as the other companies.

Let me understand the matter. Take a freight train of the Grand Trunk Railway, starting from Depot Harbour for St. John or Halifax and passing over the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Intercolonial Railway, would the freight on that train be subject to the Railway Commission for the entire journey, although it would be running for the greater part of the way on the Intercolonial Railway which is not subject to the Railway Commission. Yes.
They could not do a local freight business on the Intercolonial Railway.

Whether it be through traffic or local traffic, it would be subject to the Railway Commission upon the Intercolonial Railway, a railway which is not under the Railway Commission. It might be a difficult thing to fix rates under such conditions.

On the leased lines that is local traffic.

For points on its own line east of Montreal, but it could not take traffic along the leased lines or the operated lines to Montreal or to any intervening points.

We have to take passengers from St. John who are destined for Montreal to Moncton by the Intercolonial Railway around up to Levis, and on to Montreal, and that passenger rate is governed by the passenger rate of the Canadian Pacific Railway from St. John direct through Maine to Montreal.

The point I wanted to make is this. On the present Intercolonial Railway there are some advantages which the Intercolonial Railway gives to passengers which the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canada Atlantic Railway do not give. That is the way it stands.

Georgian bay, if they are to fix a through rate.

Halifax as well, or Sydney.

On section 5,
The terms and conditions, and the payment or compensation, upon, for or subject to which the said running powers may he so exercised shall, subject to this Act, be determined by the Board of Railway -Commissioners for Canada upon the application of the minister in accordance with the rules of procedure of the said board, subject to the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Mr. BARKER, I would like to call the hon. minister's attention to what he is going to pay for. The right he is taking is to run through freight, through passengers and do a local passenger business. It is quite possible that he may find it contrary to his best interests to do a through passenger business or a local paseuger business, but. as this clause is drawn, he will have to pay for that right or privilege whether- he afterwards chooses to exercise it or not. He will have to pay for the right. I think that a railway company would take the option to exercise al'l or any of these rights, and agree to pay for whatever portion of the rights * they should from time to time exercise.

The very definition of the word ' compensation ' refutes the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Barker). When it is determined that this right may be exercised the minister may make application to the board setting forth the powers which he would, in the interest of the railway, require to be exercised. Upon that statement the board of Railway Commissioners would determine and decide what the compensation should be. Compensation for what ? Not for all the possible rights which the minister might exercise under (this amendment, but simply compensation for the rights which he asks to be exercised. If there were no passenger business done then certainly the board would not take into consideration compensation for the permission to do a passenger business. It is only to the extent that the powers

How would you arrive at the compensation for the right of the user of that railway the extent of which is to be determined by the minister in future 1 The only fan- way to do it in the interest of the country is to agree to a payment of so much per mile for each car running upon the road. There should be no compensation in the shape of a payment for the property itself. The compensation should be fixed in the same way as was done in reference to the user of the Grand Trunk Railway bridge and terminal facilities at Montreal. If you give this wide power to the Board of Railway Commissioners or the Supreme Court to determine the value, they will do as is done in every other case where there is a joint user by different railways. A joint user means common ownership. If you have common ownership then you have to pay jointly half and half, as we do in reference to the terminal facilities and the bridge at Montreal. I understood from the right hon. leader of the government and from the hon. This clause gives a greater power to the commissioners than that. I understood further that the compensation would be fixed on the same line and on the same basis as the Railway Act provides for one railway company using another railway company's property. This clause goes further.

speechtext: and from the experience we have had of the Drummond County agreement we ought be very careful. I am sure it is not because of any want of ability that my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) has failed to grasp the intention of this Bill. He says, that it is not good business to not have a bargain prepared by the government, and then he says, that the bargain made by the government some years ago in connection with another, railway was an improvident bargain, and that the government always gets the worst of it.
Did you admit what I said to be true ?

My hon. friend is arguing both ways. The intention of this Bill is that we shall now reserve the right to exercise running powers, and I think that is a wise precaution. If it is deemed necessary in the public interest that we should take running powers then the question of the compensation shall be referred to an independent tribunal, and if the conditions imposed by that tribunal are unsatisfactory either party can take it to the Supreme Court. We all have confidence in our courts, especially in the highest court in Canada, and we need not feel any alarm as to what they may do.

When I spoke of the Drummond County deal il had in my mind that this administration has been in power for several years since that bargain was made, and having had experience they might perhaps be better able to make a good bargain for the country in the future,
My hon. friend said that no matter what bargain was made the government always got the worst of it ; he took the pessimistic view that no matter what course we took we would be worsted.

That question has come up not infrequently. I have been asked from different sections of the country to establish other branch farms. Yes ; we raise the heifers for the purpose of replenishing our own
