Will the minister explain what experiments are being carried on at these different farms ? Have we been branching out into new lines, and if so, what new lines ?
Do you give data of all these in the report ?

Yes. We have our orchard experiments at the different farms and at Indian Head and some other farms we are experimenting with trees and shrubs, and with fruit specially in British Columbia. We have 6a acres of an arboretum at Ottawa in which we have practically every known Canadian tree or shrub that will grow in this climate. We have a variety of small fruits and vegetables in connection with the orchard. Mr. Saunders just reminds me that we have been studying very carefully for some time the inoculation of the soil and the seed of clovers. The growing of clover is one of the most crucial agricultural questions, and the successful growing of clover is I may say almost a basis of successful farming in most provinces. We have made careful investigation by the chemist as well as by the outside men on the farm as to what can be
.0377

done to improve clover culture, and lately we have been inoculating, as it is called, the soil and the seed and the results have ibeen on the whole very satisfactory. We have been experimenting also as to whether the crop succeeding a clover crop was better than a crop succeeding other crops than clover, or where other grasses were sown in the place of clover. These are very important experiments and the results have been very extraordinary, as I think I! might call them, and very much to the credit of the clover crop. In regard to fruits we are trying different varieties of apples, plums and cherries, but we do not try pears here ; we have not been successful with pears at Ottawa. At Nappan we have tried them as well as apples to a certain extent, and in British Columbia of course to a large extent. We try varieties of small fruit, strawberries, raspberries, black currants, &c., and we also try different methods of culture, the results of which are published in bulletins. We experiment a good deal with fruit at Nappan and Agassiz but very little at Brandon and Indian Head although there we are doing a good deal in the way of propagating hybrids which it is hoped will supply the Northwest with an apple good for household purposes.
I have been explaining what might be called the outdoor work. Apart from that we have the indoor experimental work in the way off feeding and dealing with animals. We have dairy cows here and at Nappan, a few at Brandon and very few at Indian Head, and just enough at Agassiz to supply the farm with milk, not really enough for experimental purposes at all. At Nappan, here and at Brandon and Indian Head we every year fatten some animals, experimenting with the different methods of fattening, different feeds and with animals of different ages. The most exhaustive of these experiments are carried on here because practically the feeding of an animal indoors is much the same wherever the feeding is done. When it comes to outdoor work it is a little different. The results of these experiments serve practically for live stock men all over the country to a great extent.
Am I correct in understanding that you are not carrying on any experimental work in regard to butter and cheese on the farm ?

Not as to the making of it. We are experimenting all the time in regard to the production of milk, but as far as the making of butter and cheese is concerned we make no experiments here at all. We make up the milk at the Central Experimental Farm into butter and the same is done at Nappan. At Brandon and Indian Head there is just enough to supply the farrp hands and people like that to whom it is sold, but there is not a dairy kept there for ordinary purposes, nor is there at Agassiz. Then of course we do experimental work in the fattening of pigs and sheep as well as cattle and also some experimental work here at Ottawa in regard to the feeding of farm horses so as to try and develop some method of feeding which will be more economical than the ordinary method of feeding farm horses on Canadian farms.

I would like to ask the minister how many years the present experimental farms have been in operation and whether it would not be possible to expend less money on some of these outlying stations and thereby be able to establish others without a very great deal of extra expense ?

The farms have been established since 1886, about 17 years ; this is the 18th season I think. My hon. friend suggests that a good deal less money might be spent on these branch farms. The establishment of course was made years ago, and I have not seen my way at all clear to reduce it at any of the farms. The expenditure is increasing a little all the time owing to the increase in the rate of wages and increases of salary to men who have been a long time in the service. There has also been some little increase in the staff because we have been doing a little more work at each farm. We have also an immense amount of correspondence at all the branch farms as well as at the Central Farm which has to be handled and dealt with. The distribution of seed grain involves a very large expenditure which is constantly increasing. Then we have the sending out of the bulletins, &c., which costs a great deal and is constantly increasing.

The circulation of the bulletins in connection with these experiments is very limited. I know I have had some inquiries about this and I drew the attention, I think, of Professor Shutt to this matter and got a copy of the experiment, but I think the bulletins ought to be circulated more freely and more fairly than they are.

We have now a mailing list of over 60,000 and every bulletin is sent to 60,000 people the moment it is published and any farmer or any one else in the country who applies, has his name put on the mailing list perfectly freely, willingly and gladly.
Is the evidence taken before the Agriculture Committee sent out on the mailing list ?

No, that evidence goes to the members of parliament and the department have nothing whatever to do with it, except that each officer who gives evidence is granted the favour of having 500 copies for his own personal distribution to his friends or anybody who applies.

I cannot help feeling that since it is eighteen years since these

stations were established, and since they have not grown very materially in that time, the necessity of establishing new stations, at least small stations, in different parts of our country is certainly a matter that deserves the serious consideration of the hon. minister.

I notice large amounts at the various farms are expended for the purchase of implements, tools, &c. I would like to know if these are bought by open competition or on what system the orders are placed. There is no information on that subject.

They are placed on the judgment of the officers as to where they can get them best, as a general rule. Not infrequently, however, people send in implements and ask us to try them and then they send the bill afterwards and expect us to pay.
Mr. COCIvSHUTT. Are they always accepted in that way.
If we use them we cannot very well refuse sometimes.
If we send a few from Brantford, I hope they will be accepted in the same way.
Send us good ones and we will use them.

Would the minister say whether the live stock on the government farm pays or not ? I would also like to know whether he proposes to experiment in the breeding of horses. Some time ago an imperial army officer was over here to see whether he could get in this country different classes of horses required for the British army, including horses for cavalry and artillery. For serviceable horses to suit the different branches he would pay from $125 to $150. At present we can breed light horses, but many of them do not come up to the standard required for fancy horses. When the South African war broke out this country was flooded with horses for which there was no demand, but we shipped them over to South Africa. If the government would establish a remount depot here and give the farmers an idea of the kind of horses to breed, and if the government would bring in sires for use by the farmers in improving their stock, that would be a benefit to the agricultural community all over the Dominion.

The breeding of military horses is a matter entirely outside the experimental farm. I am glad to know there are in Canada some officers seeing what they can do in the way of purchasing horses for the War Office, but that is a matter which could not be handled in connection with experimental farms.
